title: IEnumerable and foreach
hook: foreach is not magic. It is GetEnumerator, MoveNext, Current, and dispose if the enumerator is IDisposable. IEnumerable<T> is the sequence contract the rest of the BCL speaks.

sections.heading: The foreach pattern
sections.prose: Microsoft’s iteration-statement docs: foreach works on IEnumerable / IEnumerable<T>, and also on any type with a public GetEnumerator whose return has Current and MoveNext(). GetEnumerator may be an extension method. If Current is a ref return, the iteration variable can be ref. An empty collection skips the body. A null collection throws NullReferenceException — annotate the parameter as IEnumerable<T> not IEnumerable<T>? if you already guarded. List<T>.Enumerator is a struct; foreach on List avoids boxing that enumerator. foreach on IEnumerable<T> boxes it. That is why APIs that take IEnumerable<T> are flexible and sometimes slower. Do not mutate a List while foreach is running; the version counter throws InvalidOperationException.

snippets.label: foreach over a batch
snippets.explanation: The method accepts any sequence. Null is a throw, not an empty loop. Async sequences are a different interface.

sections.heading: IEnumerable<T> versus IReadOnlyList<T>
sections.prose: IEnumerable<T> promises you can walk it, not that you can Count in O(1) or index. LINQ Count() may enumerate the whole thing. If you need a snapshot with indexer, take IReadOnlyList<T> or T[]. Returning IEnumerable<T> from a public API hides whether you allocated a List or a yield iterator — which is good for flexibility and bad when callers enumerate twice (next topic). ICollection<T> and IList<T> add mutation; prefer the read-only interfaces on outputs.

sections.heading: Variance is later
sections.prose: IEnumerable<out T> is covariant: IEnumerable<string> can be passed where IEnumerable<object> is expected. That is why foreach (object o in strings) is legal. The in/out rules, how they differ from TypeScript, and why IList<T> is invariant wait for module 09. Here, treat IEnumerable<T> as “a sequence of T.”

interviewTakeaways: foreach is MoveNext/Current, plus Dispose when the enumerator is disposable.
IEnumerable<T> is walkable, not necessarily a materialized list.
await foreach / IAsyncEnumerable<T> is module 13, not a foreach flag.
commonPitfalls: Passing a null list into foreach and calling it an empty batch.
Using IEnumerable<T> in a tight inner loop where you needed IReadOnlyList<T> for Count and indexer.

jsTsCorrelations.note: for...of uses Symbol.iterator. C# foreach uses GetEnumerator. Both can be backed by generators/iterators.
TS Iterable<T> is the structural cousin of IEnumerable<T>, erased at run time. IEnumerable<T> is a real CLR interface.
